query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build substrate during selective laser melting of high‐entropy alloy components will reduce the thermal gradients that cause residual stresses and microstructural defects, thereby enhancing dimensional precision and mechanical integrity compared to parts built on a room‐temperature substrate.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built high-entropy alloy components (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn) produced via SLM using conventional processing parameters with a room-temperature substrate, which typically exhibit residual stress‐induced distortions and fabrication defects.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled pre-heating strategy by raising the build substrate temperature to a predetermined set-point during the SLM process.
generation.conditions: Processing under standard SLM parameters and atmospheric conditions with the only change being the substrate pre-heated to a controlled temperature (controlled variable) during fabrication. Post-fabrication evaluations should be performed using dimensional metrology, mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests, hardness measurements), and microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM) under ambient testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduced thermal gradient between the melt pool and surrounding material leads to lower residual stress, fewer microstructural defects (e.g., porosity and hot cracks), and a more uniform grain structure.
generation.mechanism: By preheating the build substrate, the steep temperature drop during and after laser scanning is minimized. This reduction in cooling rate and thermal shock decreases contraction-induced stresses and minimizes defects associated with rapid solidification, thereby improving the overall dimensional accuracy and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Dimensional deviations will be reduced and mechanical integrity (e.g., yield strength and fracture toughness) will be improved relative to the baseline; however, the exact magnitude of improvement remains uncertain until experimentally quantified.
generation.baseline: SLM-fabricated high-entropy alloy components produced under standard conditions (room-temperature substrate) that show noticeable residual stresses, microstructural defects, and dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.boundary: The expected benefits are tied to the specific HEA composition and SLM processing conditions; results may vary if the alloy composition or processing environment deviates significantly from the tested scenario.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in strength and dimensional accuracy are not defined ahead of experiments and may depend on the optimal pre-heating temperature and its interaction with other processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of identical high-entropy alloy components via SLM using the same laser and scanning parameters: one set with the substrate at room temperature (control) and one set with a pre-heated substrate. After fabrication, perform dimensional measurements using a coordinate measuring machine, conduct tensile tests and hardness measurements, and analyze microstructural features (porosity, cracks) by SEM.
measurements: Tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the components produced with the pre-heated substrate do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, mechanical properties, or a reduced defect density compared to the control group, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study uniquely demonstrates the processability, hot-cracking susceptibility, and in situ mechanical response of CoCrFeNiCu-HEA fabricated by L-PBF, providing new insights into defect evolution and mechanical performance under these specific processing conditions. Future work will focus on targeted alloying (e.g., Al addition), pre-heating strategies, and optimized scanning to further reduce hot-cracking susceptibility and enhance mechanical performance. This study provides insights into the processability, defect evolution, and mechanical response of L-PBF CoCrFeNiCu-HEA, guiding the development of crack-resistant, additively manufactured HEAs.

It has been highlighted that even small changes in processing parameters have a significant effect on the physical properties and microstructure of the final parts [], and even give rise to major defects in the parts, e.g., unreasonable process parameters [], internal defects induced by incomplete laser scanning filling [], geometric defects and macroscopic deformations under residual stress generated by apparent thermal gradients in the manufacturing process [], severe notching or deformation of the support bar. The literature [] illustrates the causes of these defects and concludes that the mechanical and biological properties of the parts are seriously affected. It is also found in the literature [] that the fatigue life of SLMed parts under multi-axle load is significantly reduced due to stress concentration caused by internal defects compared to forgings and that defects also affect the manufacturability, dimensional accuracy and surface roughness of SLM lattice structure [].
